stops.name: Crystal Hot Springs
stops.tag: Developed hot & cold pools · Honeyville, UT
stops.desc: A family-run hot springs resort with several mineral soaking pools ranging from warm to very hot, plus a large cold pool and waterslide, right on I-15 north of Brigham City.
stops.note: About 13 miles north of Brigham City on the way out, Crystal Hot Springs channels natural mineral water into a range of developed pools from cool to scalding, plus a large recreational pool and waterslide — an easy first soak of the trip, right off I-15.
stops.credit: Illustrative rendering — exact pools not photographed

stops.name: Malad: Lottery Ticket Stop
stops.tag: 27 Bannock St · first town over the Idaho line
stops.desc: The first town across the Idaho line — and the closest place for Utahns to buy a lottery ticket, since Utah is one of only a few states with no lottery at all.
stops.note: Utah has no state lottery, so whenever Powerball or Mega Millions climbs toward a big jackpot, Utahns make the short drive north across the border to Malad City to buy tickets — gas stations here, especially KJ's Kwik Stop on Main Street, regularly see lines of Utah plates. Malad City is also the seat of Oneida County, settled in the 1860s largely by Welsh immigrants — it's said to have more residents of Welsh descent per capita than anywhere in the U.S. outside Wales. The Oneida Pioneer Museum and 1917 courthouse anchor its small historic downtown a block away.

stops.name: Devil Creek Reservoir
stops.desc: A small high-desert reservoir just off I-15, popular with anglers and an easy stretch-the-legs stop.
stops.address: Devil Creek Reservoir, near I-15 Exit 22, Malad, ID
stops.note: Tucked into a break in the mountains just north of Malad Pass, Devil Creek Reservoir is stocked with rainbow trout by Idaho Fish & Game. It sits right alongside the highway, with views back down the Malad Valley.

stops.name: McCammon
stops.desc: A small railroad town where the route leaves the interstate for Lava Hot Springs.
stops.note: McCammon grew up in 1892 as the junction of the Oregon Short Line Railroad and the Utah & Northern Railway, earning it the old nickname "Junction City." It still carries some of that railroad-town character, including the historic Harkness Hotel, and marks the turnoff from I-15 onto US-30 toward Lava Hot Springs.

stops.name: Lava Hot Springs
stops.tag: Main Street · World Famous Hot Pools
stops.desc: Idaho's favorite soak for over a century — odorless mineral pools tucked below the canyon, an Olympic-size swim complex with waterslides next door, and a walkable Main Street along the Portneuf River. The turnaround point of the day.
stops.address: 430 E Main St, Lava Hot Springs, ID 83246
stops.note: The mineral hot pools here have drawn visitors for well over a century; the Shoshone-Bannock people are said to have treated the springs as neutral, sacred ground where rival tribes could bathe in peace. Today the state-run Hot Pools sit alongside a separate Olympic-size swimming pool and waterslide complex on the Portneuf River, with Main Street's shops and cafes a short walk away — the turnaround point of the day.

stops.name: Soda Springs Geyser
stops.desc: The world's only captive, human-triggered geyser, erupting roughly 100 feet on the hour — in a town first known as an Oregon Trail rest stop, later formally settled by Mormon pioneers.
stops.note: Soda Springs was settled long before the geyser existed. Native Americans and fur trappers knew its bubbling mineral springs for generations, and it became a well-known 'Oregon Trail Oasis' where 1800s emigrants paused to bathe, drink the naturally carbonated water, and rest. Colonel Patrick Connor established an early army post and settlement, Morristown, near here in 1863; in 1870, Brigham Young formally founded present-day Soda Springs just east of that site as one of his planned Mormon colonies. Decades later, in 1937, drillers looking for a warm-water swimming pool accidentally tapped a pressurized aquifer, creating the geyser so powerful the town had to cap it with a valve — it's now set on a timer to erupt roughly on the hour at Geyser Park downtown.

stops.name: Hooper Springs Park
stops.tag: Government Dam Rd · naturally carbonated spring
stops.desc: A quiet park just north of downtown with a spring of naturally carbonated mineral water you can drink from the source.
stops.address: 1805 Government Dam Rd, Soda Springs, ID 83276
stops.note: Hooper Spring was a documented stop on the Oregon and California Trails, where westbound emigrants paused to sample the naturally carbonated "soda" water the town is named for. A small stone pavilion still covers the spring today, and the shaded park around it makes a pleasant short break — about 2 miles north of the geyser, barely off the direct route.

stops.name: Bear River Massacre Site
stops.tag: US-91 near Preston · National Historic Landmark
stops.desc: A solemn overlook and monument marking the deadliest single episode of violence between the U.S. Army and Native Americans in the West — fought between Colonel Patrick Edward Connor's California Volunteers and the Northwestern Shoshone led by Chief Bear Hunter.
stops.note: On January 29, 1863, roughly 200 California Volunteer troops under Colonel Patrick Edward Connor attacked a Northwestern Shoshone winter camp led by Chief Bear Hunter, encamped along the Bear River. Estimates of Shoshone deaths range from about 250 up to 400–500 men, women, and children, while the Army reported 21–23 soldiers killed and roughly 50 more wounded — a toll higher than at Sand Creek or Wounded Knee, making it the deadliest single episode of violence between the U.S. Army and Native Americans in the West. A 1932 monument and newer interpretive panels, developed with the Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation, mark the bluff overlooking the site, directly on the route into Preston.

stops.name: Preston — Historic Downtown
stops.desc: Franklin County's seat, and the real small town where the film Napoleon Dynamite was shot in 2003.
stops.note: Preston's unassuming downtown — including the Franklin County Courthouse, the old Deseret Industries thrift store, and Preston High School — became familiar to millions after Napoleon Dynamite was filmed here on a shoestring budget in 2003. Fans still stop for tater tots and to spot Rex Kwon Do landmarks.

stops.name: Bear River Hot Springs
stops.tag: Riverside soaking pools · short detour from Preston
stops.desc: A rustic, family-run soak on the Bear River just northeast of Preston — simple mineral pools right on the riverbank, open year-round.
stops.note: A low-key, family-owned hot springs resort on the banks of the Bear River, with mineral soaking pools open year-round (hours vary by day). A short detour northeast of downtown Preston, it's a quieter alternative to Lava for a soak on the way home.
stops.credit: Illustrative rendering — exact pools not photographed

stops.name: Maple Grove Hot Springs
stops.tag: Riverside pools & glamping · via ID-34 from Preston
stops.desc: A scenic 45-acre riverside property with several soaking pools, a sandy beach, and glamping — about a 21-mile detour up ID-34 from Preston.
stops.note: Tucked into a river canyon along ID-34, Maple Grove is a 45-acre soaking retreat with four to six riverside mineral pools, a beach, hiking trails, and glamping yurts and cabins. It's farther off-route than the other springs — worth it only if there's time for the full detour.
stops.credit: Illustrative rendering — exact pools not photographed

stops.name: Logan
stops.desc: Cache Valley's college town, settled by Mormon pioneers in the 1850s in a valley named decades earlier by fur trappers and mountain men who cached their pelts here.
stops.note: Cache Valley gets its name from the fur-trapping era of the 1820s: mountain men working for outfits like William Ashley's Rocky Mountain Fur Company wintered in the valley and cached — buried or hid — their beaver pelts and supplies here rather than hauling them out, and the valley hosted a famous trappers' rendezvous in 1826. Early arrivals had called it "Willow Valley" for its riverbank willows, but the cache name stuck. Mormon pioneers settled the valley permanently in the 1850s, founding Logan and, between 1878 and 1891, building the grand limestone Logan Tabernacle that still anchors Main Street today, with the larger Logan Temple visible on the bench above.

stops.name: Brigham City
stops.desc: Home to the 1890 Box Elder Tabernacle, famous for its 15 hand-carved "candlestick" spires — and just down the road from legendary Maddox Ranch House, closed on this Sunday.
stops.address: 251 S Main St, Brigham City, UT 84302
stops.note: The original Box Elder Tabernacle burned in 1896 and was rebuilt within a year; its distinctive candlestick-topped tower and spires make it one of the most photographed buildings in northern Utah, anchoring Brigham City's poplar-lined Main Street. Just south in nearby Perry, Maddox Ranch House Restaurant has served its famous fried chicken and steaks since 1949 — but it's closed Sundays and Mondays, so it won't be an option on this Sunday drive. Brigham City is the last stop before this drive rejoins I-15 south toward Murray.

stops.name: Ogden — Union Station
stops.tag: Historic 25th Street · railroad, gun & car museums
stops.desc: This 1924 Spanish Colonial Revival depot anchors historic 25th Street, once one of the West's busiest rail junctions. Today it houses railroad, firearms, and classic-car museums under grand arched windows — a quick, walkable stop with easy access to Ogden's best restaurants and shops.
stops.note: Opened in 1924 after fire destroyed its predecessor, Union Station once saw dozens of trains a day pass through Ogden's rail junction connecting the transcontinental line. The restored depot now houses the Utah State Railroad, Browning Firearms, and Browning-Kimball classic-car museums beneath its grand arched windows, with the shops, galleries, and restaurants of historic 25th Street a short walk away — a good last stretch-the-legs stop before the freeway home. Ogden's rail yards also drew large numbers of Greek immigrants in the early 1900s, who lived and worked section and steel gangs on the Oregon Short Line and Union Pacific out of the city — part of the same wave of Greek railroad and mining labor that built Greektowns across Utah.
